title: The Microscope That Made Curiosity Independent

scenes.text: A microscope can be more than an instrument. Mine changed when and where I could look, long before it changed what I understood.
I bought it near Qasr El Einy in Cairo. Bringing it to Qatar took effort. No one had assigned me this instrument.
By July first, twenty seventeen, a photograph showed the microscope on my desk at home in Qatar, beside books, notes, and a chemistry mug.
University laboratories rightly have protocols and schedules. At home I could follow a question without waiting for a reserved session or a class.
On vacation mornings, a lens was always within reach. I could stop, adjust the focus, revisit a preparation, and let curiosity choose the hour.
The temptation is to call every view a discovery. But seeing is not knowing. Interpretation still demands controls, careful preparation, and doubt.
This personal microscope did not produce the findings of my later collaborative studies. Those results depended on other instruments, colleagues, and protocols.
Something quieter changed: paying attention became a daily habit, not just a scheduled activity. That difference stayed with me.
I brought a microscope from Cairo. In Qatar, it became a way to look independently—and to ask, every time, what I was really seeing.
